prohibited_recommendations: Do not give haloperidol or other high-potency D2 antagonists for agitation: patients with anti-NMDAR encephalitis are prone to severe extrapyramidal and neuroleptic-malignant-like reactions.
Do not delay immunotherapy while waiting for the anti-NMDAR antibody result when clinical probability is high: antibody turnaround can take 1 to 2 weeks and delay worsens outcome.
Do not attribute the presentation to a primary psychiatric disorder while seizures, dyskinesias, autonomic instability, an abnormal EEG or CSF inflammation remain unexplained.
Do not perform lumbar puncture without prior imaging in a patient with altered consciousness, focal signs, or new seizures: exclude mass effect first.
Do not interpret a negative serum anti-NMDAR antibody as ruling out the disease; the CSF assay is the gold standard and may be positive when serum is negative.
required_recommendations: Start IV acyclovir 10 mg/kg every 8 hours at presentation, and stop it once CSF HSV PCR is negative and the antibody diagnosis is established; repeat the PCR on a second CSF sample if the first LP was within 72 hours of onset and HSV encephalitis remains plausible. Hold ibuprofen and other NSAIDs while IV acyclovir is given.

Start first-line immunotherapy without waiting for the antibody result once infection is reasonably excluded: IV methylprednisolone 1 g daily for 5 days with IVIG 0.4 g/kg/day for 5 days (2 g/kg total) or plasma exchange (5 to 7 exchanges).
Arrange prompt surgical removal of the left ovarian teratoma (laparoscopic, ovary-sparing where feasible) as part of first-line treatment, with gynecology.
Treat seizures with an antiseizure medication such as levetiracetam or lacosamide; avoid valproate in a woman able to become pregnant; seizures respond mainly to immunotherapy.
Monitor with continuous EEG for non-convulsive seizures while consciousness fluctuates or seizures persist.
Admit to the ICU / neurocritical care for autonomic instability (labile blood pressure with diaphoresis, heart rate 114 bpm) and recurrent seizures, with airway assessment and cardiac monitoring.

If there is no meaningful clinical improvement 10 to 14 days after first-line therapy, escalate to rituximab (375 mg/m² weekly for 4 doses or 1 g twice 2 weeks apart, after hepatitis B screening) and/or cyclophosphamide; discuss fertility preservation before cyclophosphamide.
Treat agitation and insomnia with benzodiazepines (lorazepam, titrated from the current 0.5 mg dose) first.
Neurology-led care with psychiatry for behavioral management; gynecology for the teratoma.

avoided_actions.rationale: Transthoracic echo is not indicated for anti-NMDAR encephalitis; it adds cost without informing diagnosis or management unless a discrete cardiac concern (e.g., new murmur, embolic stroke) coexists.
EMG/NCS plays no role in the diagnostic workup of anti-NMDAR encephalitis; it neither confirms the antibody-mediated CNS process nor distinguishes among the differential diagnoses.
Amyloid PET targets Alzheimer pathology and contributes no information to the diagnosis or treatment of autoimmune encephalitis in a young patient with subacute neuropsychiatric symptoms.

DaTscan evaluates nigrostriatal dopaminergic function and has no role in autoimmune encephalitis; the orofacial dyskinesias of anti-NMDAR encephalitis are antibody-mediated, not presynaptic dopaminergic.

differential.key_features: Oromandibular automatisms with post-event confusion, word-finding difficulty, autonomic lability, left temporal sharp waves with electrographic seizures, CSF pleocytosis and CSF anti-GluN1 positive.
The benzodiazepine on the urine screen is the prescribed lorazepam 0.5 mg, started after the illness began; no clonus or hyperthermia; CK 142 U/L.

Her migraines are without aura and her husband says this illness is entirely unlike them; migraine does not explain a 12-day encephalopathy with electrographic seizures, autonomic lability and CSF anti-GluN1 antibodies.

key_clinical_evidence: Twelve days of insomnia, fear and paranoia, fragmented speech with word-finding difficulty, staring spells and an oromandibular automatism with post-event confusion, tremor with increased tone, and labile blood pressure with diaphoresis three weeks after a febrile cold: at least five of the six Graus 2016 groups.
CSF IgG anti-GluN1 positive (titer 1:20) on cell-based assay: definite anti-NMDAR encephalitis (Graus 2016); serum positive 1:40 is read with the CSF.

MRI shows subtle left hippocampal and amygdala FLAIR signal without restricted diffusion or hemorrhage; MRI is normal or non-specific in about two thirds and excludes HSV encephalitis and structural causes.

EEG shows left temporal sharp waves and slowing, and continuous EEG captures five left temporal seizures and extreme delta brush; extreme delta brush, when present, supports but does not establish the diagnosis.
Pelvic ultrasound shows a 2.8 cm left ovarian mature cystic teratoma: its removal is part of first-line treatment.
Earlier immunotherapy and tumor removal are associated with better outcome (Titulaer 2013).

alternatives: Paracetamol in place of ibuprofen for headache or fever while on IV acyclovir.
contraindications: Class warning: haloperidol and other high-potency dopamine D2 antagonists are associated with severe extrapyramidal and neuroleptic malignant-like reactions in anti-NMDA receptor encephalitis.
Valproate: avoid in women able to become pregnant unless other options fail.
interactions: Ibuprofen (current, as needed) with IV acyclovir: additive nephrotoxicity; avoid NSAIDs while acyclovir is given and keep the patient hydrated.
Ibuprofen with high-dose methylprednisolone: increased risk of gastrointestinal bleeding; avoid the combination or add gastric protection.
Lorazepam (current) with further benzodiazepine doses or other sedatives: additive sedation and respiratory depression.
Sumatriptan (as needed): no clinically relevant interaction with the acute agents; serotonergic, so review if serotonergic drugs are added.
IVIG: risk of renal impairment and thrombosis; ensure hydration and avoid rapid infusion rates.
High-dose methylprednisolone: hyperglycemia, hypertension and hypokalemia; monitor glucose and electrolytes.
Levetiracetam: no clinically relevant pharmacokinetic interactions; renally cleared.
general.summary: Ibuprofen, sumatriptan and lorazepam reviewed against the acute agents; NSAIDs add nephrotoxicity with acyclovir and bleeding risk with steroids. Class cautions listed above.
warnings: Rituximab: screen for hepatitis B (HBsAg, anti-HBc) before the first dose.
Cyclophosphamide is gonadotoxic and teratogenic: discuss fertility preservation and contraception.
Sulfonamide allergy (rash): none of the agents above is a sulfonamide.

anti-NMDA receptor encephalitis diagnosi.query: anti-NMDA receptor encephalitis diagnosis and treatment

results.finding: Definite anti-NMDAR encephalitis requires one or more of six major symptom groups and IgG anti-GluN1 antibodies, with CSF testing included; probable disease requires four groups (or three with a teratoma) of rapid onset plus an abnormal EEG or CSF pleocytosis or oligoclonal bands.
results.source: Graus F et al. Lancet Neurol 2016;15:391-404

results.finding: All patients had antibodies in CSF, whereas about 14% were negative in serum; CSF titers related more closely to outcome than serum titers.
results.source: Gresa-Arribas N et al. Lancet Neurol 2014;13:167-177

results.finding: 38% had a tumor, mostly ovarian teratoma; 53% improved within 4 weeks of first-line immunotherapy or tumor removal; second-line rituximab or cyclophosphamide after first-line failure was associated with better outcome; 81% had mRS 0-2 at 24 months.
results.source: Titulaer MJ et al. Lancet Neurol 2013;12:157-165

results.finding: Extreme delta brush was found in 7 of 23 adults with anti-NMDAR encephalitis and was associated with a more prolonged illness.

anti-NMDA receptor encephalitis diagnosi.summary: Published criteria and cohort data on anti-NMDA receptor encephalitis: definite diagnosis rests on CSF IgG anti-GluN1 antibodies; first-line immunotherapy and tumor removal are followed by second-line agents when there is no response.

patient.history_present_illness: A 30-year-old right-handed Hispanic woman was brought to the emergency department by her husband who reports that over the past 10 days she has undergone a dramatic personality change that he describes as completely out of character. She is a school teacher and was in her normal state of health until approximately 12 days ago when she began complaining of difficulty sleeping, restlessness, and feeling 'on edge.' Over the subsequent days she became increasingly fearful that someone was watching the family home and began insisting her husband lock all the windows and doors at specific times. She refused to allow the children to go to school, stating she 'had a feeling something bad would happen.' Her speech became progressively more fragmented and she began having long periods of staring blankly at the wall, unresponsive to her husband calling her name. He took her to their primary care physician five days ago who attributed the symptoms to anxiety and stress and prescribed lorazepam 0.5 mg. The lorazepam provided minimal benefit and she continued to deteriorate. She has not slept more than 1-2 hours per night for the past week. On the day of presentation she had an episode where she appeared to be chewing and making repetitive lip movements for about 30 seconds, after which she was confused for several minutes. This alarmed her husband who brought her to the ED. She has a history of migraines but her husband states this presentation is entirely unlike any migraine she has had before. She had a mild cold with low-grade fever approximately 3 weeks ago that lasted about one week. No recent travel. Last menstrual period was 3 weeks ago; she is not pregnant.

neurological_exam.additional: No nuchal rigidity. Mild tachycardia and blood pressure lability noted. Intermittent mild diaphoresis.
neurological_exam.coordination: Finger-nose slightly dysmetric bilaterally; may be due to tremor.
neurological_exam.cranial_nerves: Pupils 3mm, equal, reactive. Extraocular movements intact without nystagmus. Mild facial asymmetry with right lower facial droop (new per husband). Tongue midline.
neurological_exam.gait: Wide-based, cautious gait. No ataxia on tandem.
neurological_exam.mental_status: Alert but confused. Oriented to person only. Responds to simple commands inconsistently. Speech is fragmented with word-finding difficulty. Intermittent periods of blank staring lasting 15-30 seconds with unresponsiveness. Periodic lip-smacking and oromandibular automatisms observed during examination.
neurological_exam.motor: Mild bilateral upper extremity tremor at rest. Tone mildly increased bilaterally. Full strength 5/5 in all extremities on manual testing.
neurological_exam.sensory: Grossly intact to light touch. Limited cooperation for detailed sensory exam.
